741.event_title: Edward I builds his castles in north Wales
741.event: After conquering the last independent part of Wales, King Edward I of England began building great castles at Conwy, Caernarfon and Harlech in 1283, and later at Beaumaris, largely designed by his chief military architect, James of St George. UNESCO describes them as works of both colonisation and defence. Harlech stood on a crag above the sea with access to a small quay, so that in times of trouble it could be supplied by boat, and it was attacked during the Welsh rising led by Madog ap Llywelyn in 1294-95.
741.explanation: The castles served Edward both as bases from which his officials and soldiers controlled newly conquered country and as strongholds where garrisons, supplied from the sea, could hold out when the Welsh rose against them.
741.tie_back: The kural says a fortress is precious both to the king who marches out to attack and to the one who shelters behind it in fear, and Edward's castles were built to serve exactly both purposes.
741._accuracy_note: Strong fit, since the castles were explicitly instruments of conquest and places of refuge at once, though the event is a building programme rather than a single dramatic moment.

742.event_title: Rajput rulers build the hill forts of Rajasthan among hills, rivers, forest and desert
742.event: Between the 8th and 18th centuries the Rajput states of Rajasthan built a series of great hill forts, six of which, at Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer, now form a single UNESCO World Heritage property. UNESCO notes that the forts use the natural defences offered by the landscape, namely hills, deserts, rivers and dense forests, with Ranthambore set in forest, Gagron protected by a river and Jaisalmer standing in desert, and that they contain extensive water-harvesting structures. Gagron is surrounded on three sides by the waters of the Ahu and Kalisindh rivers.
742.explanation: The forts show a long South Asian tradition of choosing sites where water, hills, forest and open ground did much of the work of defence, backed by secure water supplies.
742.tie_back: Valluvar lists clear water, open ground, hills and dense forest as the marks of a true fortress, and the Rajput builders set their forts among exactly these natural defences.
742._accuracy_note: Very close fit, since the kural's own list of natural defences matches UNESCO's description, though the event is a long building tradition rather than one dated moment.

743.event_title: Theodosius II builds the land walls of Constantinople
743.event: Under Emperor Theodosius II and his prefect Anthemius, a new line of land walls was built across the peninsula of Constantinople, with work dated to about 413 and repeatedly strengthened afterwards. The system combined a massive main wall with 96 towers, a lower outer wall in front of it and a moat. World History Encyclopedia gives the inner wall as almost 5 metres thick and about 12 metres high, with a moat about 20 metres wide that could be flooded, an arrangement that kept enemy siege engines far from the main wall.
743.explanation: The layered walls protected Constantinople through many sieges over the following centuries and became the classic example of a city defence that height, thickness and obstacles made almost impossible to approach.
743.tie_back: The kural names height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility as the four qualities of a fortress wall, and the Theodosian walls combined tall towers, thick masonry and a moat that kept attackers at a distance.
743._accuracy_note: Close illustration of all four qualities of a wall, although the precise dimensions come from one of the two sources.

744.event_title: The garrison of Kumamoto Castle holds out against the Satsuma army
744.event: In February 1877, during the Satsuma Rebellion, Saigo Takamori's samurai army attacked Kumamoto Castle, the only Imperial Army base in Kyushu, which was defended by government troops under Major General Tani Tateki. The castle had been built in the early 1600s by Kato Kiyomasa as a formidable fortress, and this was the first time its defences were tested in battle. The garrison held the castle for about two months without the rebels getting in, until government reinforcements arrived in April and the Satsuma forces withdrew.
744.explanation: Although the Satsuma forces were seasoned fighters and the defenders were less experienced, the castle let the garrison hold out until the rebel offensive lost its momentum and was broken.
744.tie_back: The kural praises a fort that is easy to guard yet roomy within and that breaks the spirit of any enemy who attacks it, and Kumamoto Castle stalled the rebel army until its campaign collapsed.
744._accuracy_note: Good on a fort wearing down the attackers' momentum, but the sources do not detail the specific design of a short perimeter around a large interior that the kural stresses.

745.event_title: Hunger forces the surrender of Vicksburg
745.event: The Confederate army under General John Pemberton had spent more than a year fortifying Vicksburg with a ring of earthen forts and over 170 cannon, and two Union assaults ordered by General Ulysses S. Grant on 19 and 22 May 1863 failed to break through. Grant then laid siege to the city and cut it off from supplies, and the defenders' daily rations shrank to tiny portions of bacon, flour, sugar, peas and molasses. After 47 days of siege, Pemberton's army surrendered on 4 July 1863.
745.explanation: Vicksburg showed that earthworks and guns could repel direct assault but not hunger; once its food ran short, the stronghold that controlled the Mississippi had to yield.
745.tie_back: The kural asks that a fort be hard to capture, well stocked with food and easy for its defenders to hold; Vicksburg had the first and third qualities but not the second, and fell for that lack.
745._accuracy_note: Strong illustration by negative example, since the defences held against assault but the food supply did not.

746.event_title: King George VI awards the George Cross to the island of Malta
746.event: From 1940 Malta was under almost constant air attack, and from January to July 1942 there was only one 24-hour period when no bombs fell; food, fuel and ammunition ran so short that the people came close to starvation and spent long periods in underground shelters. On 15 April 1942 King George VI awarded the George Cross to the island and its people in recognition of their courage under repeated attack. Later in 1942 the Operation Pedestal convoy fought its way through to Malta with vital supplies, despite the loss of many of its ships.
746.explanation: Malta's survival depended on both supplies brought in at great cost and the endurance of the people who held on under bombardment.
746.tie_back: Valluvar says a true fortress holds every needed thing and has brave people who help when danger comes, and the island fortress of Malta survived only when both came together.
746._accuracy_note: Close fit to the kural's pairing of stores and brave defenders, with the island itself serving as the fortress.

747.event_title: Krak des Chevaliers falls to Sultan Baybars
747.event: Krak des Chevaliers, the great Hospitaller castle regarded as virtually impregnable, was besieged by the Mamluk sultan Baybars from early 1271. His army pounded the walls with siege engines and used miners to bring down a tower, breaking into the outer ward, but the defenders held out in the stronger inner castle. On 8 April 1271 the remaining garrison surrendered after receiving a letter ordering them to do so, which the French Ministry of Culture's account describes as forged by Baybars and World History Encyclopedia describes as perhaps forged.
747.explanation: Where siege and assault had only partly succeeded against one of the finest castles ever built, deception completed the conquest.
747.tie_back: The kural lists the three ways a fort may be taken, by siege, by direct assault and by treachery, and at Krak des Chevaliers all three were used, the last one finishing the work.
747._accuracy_note: Near-dramatisation of the kural's three methods, though the sources differ on how certain the forgery is and whose name it bore, which the entry reflects.

748.event_title: The Rats of Tobruk hold the port against Rommel
748.event: In April 1941 a German-Italian army under General Erwin Rommel surrounded the Libyan port of Tobruk, which was held by a garrison of mainly Australian troops under Lieutenant General Leslie Morshead, together with British and Indian units. The defenders, supplied by night by Royal Navy and Royal Australian Navy ships, held a long defensive perimeter, patrolled aggressively and repulsed repeated ground assaults under almost constant shelling and bombing. The siege ended in December 1941 without the Axis forces taking the port, and the soldiers adopted as a badge of honour the name Rats of Tobruk, first used as a taunt by German propaganda.
748.explanation: Holding Tobruk forced the Axis to bring most of their supplies overland across some 1,500 kilometres of desert and helped keep them from Egypt and the Suez Canal.
748.tie_back: The kural says a true fortress lets defenders who hold fast to their positions defeat even a strong army skilled in siegecraft, and the Tobruk garrison's refusal to give up ground defeated one of the war's most capable commanders.
748._accuracy_note: Very close fit to defenders holding their ground against a skilled besieger, though Tobruk was a fortified port rather than a single fortress.

749.event: During the British invasion of the Zulu Kingdom, after the British defeat at Isandlwana on 22 January 1879, the small garrison at the mission station of Rorke's Drift, led by Lieutenants John Chard and Gonville Bromhead, chose to stay and fight rather than retreat. They built barricades from bags of maize, biscuit boxes and other stores and held off attacks by a Zulu force several thousand strong from late afternoon until dawn. Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded to the defenders.
749.explanation: The improvised post became one of the most celebrated actions in British military memory, remembered far more widely than the larger defeat that came just before it.
749.tie_back: Valluvar says a fortress wins its fame through the deeds of its defenders at the battle front, and Rorke's Drift, not even a true fort, became famous solely for the stand made there.
749._accuracy_note: Strong fit on fame earned by defenders' deeds; the event belongs to a colonial war of conquest, which the entry states plainly.

750.event_title: Fort Douaumont falls almost without a shot
750.event: Fort Douaumont, the largest and one of the most modern of the forts guarding Verdun, had been stripped of most of its guns and much of its garrison in 1915 on the orders of the French high command. When German troops approached it on 25 February 1916, only a small body of reserve gunners remained inside. A German sergeant found his way in through one of the gun embrasures, other small parties followed, and the fort was taken without a real fight.
750.explanation: Douaumont showed that even the most modern fortress was worthless once too few capable defenders were left inside to use it, and its easy fall shocked France early in the Battle of Verdun.
750.tie_back: The kural ends the chapter by saying that however excellent a fortress may be, it is no fortress at all without people of skill and vigour to hold it, and Douaumont is almost a literal case.
750._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a superb fortress lost because it lacked men to defend it.
